D.3 What must be supplied to submit this document

Everything in this thesis is generated from the repository except the information below, which is about the submission rather than about the science and cannot be derived or guessed. It is collected in one file, paper/00_institution.yaml. Filling that file and re-running build_thesis.py generates the title page, the declaration, the supervisor’s approval block and the signature lines; no other part of the manuscript needs editing. Any field left unfilled renders as a visible bracketed placeholder rather than a silent blank, so an incomplete page is obvious.

Required:

  1. Author’s full name, exactly as it must appear on the title page.
  2. Student or registration number.
  3. Degree title, in the institution’s own wording — for example “Bachelor of Science in Biotechnology”.
  4. Department, faculty and full institution name.
  5. City and country.
  6. Supervisor’s name and title, and a co-supervisor’s if there is one.
  7. Month and year of submission, and the academic year.
  8. Declaration language — English, Arabic, or both. The thesis already carries abstracts in both.

Required if the institution provides one:

  1. The Word template. Placed at paper/template.docx, it is used as pandoc’s reference document and carries the institution’s fonts, margins, heading styles and page numbering into the build automatically. If only a written specification exists rather than a file, recording it in template_notes is enough for someone to apply it by hand in one pass.

Worth confirming, because conventions differ and this analysis has no way to know:

  1. Whether a reference style is mandated. The reference list is generated by src/build_references.py from a structured bibliography, so a required style can be applied by changing one function rather than by editing 230 entries.
  2. Whether the institution requires a declaration of AI or computational tool use. The thesis states in its front matter that the work is entirely computational and reproducible from the repository, which may or may not satisfy a specific local wording.

Appendix E — The verification record

This appendix records what the verification passes found. It is kept in the document rather than in a repository note because several of the faults it lists are the kind that survive peer review undetected, and because the last item is the only task in the thesis that cannot be completed from the repository.

  1. Re-resolve every DOI in the bibliography. Done, and worth recording for what it found, because every fault below would otherwise have become a wrong in-text citation.

    The titre corpus: 295 of 306 identifiers resolved cleanly, but 62 rows, a fifth of the corpus, carried the wrong first author despite a correct DOI, and one carried the wrong year. A row citing Rantasalo was a paper whose first author is Mojzita; four citing Zhang in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry were Hu; three citing Zhang in the Journal of Fungi were Panchanawaporn. All corrections are in data/literature/reference_corrections.md.

    The bibliography: 189 of 230 entries now carry a DOI resolved against Crossref and confirmed independently at doi.org, up from 141 before the pass. Rebuilding each entry from registry metadata changed 49 author lists, 11 first authors, 12 years, 3 truncated titles and 1 venue, and a second pass recovered 48 identifiers by title search, accepted only above 0.97 title similarity with year, first author and registry type all agreeing and the DOI confirmed live. That pass corrected two further records and exposed two papers this bibliography had listed twice, now merged. The 41 entries that remain without an identifier legitimately have none, and three whose automated verdict was “no record” were searched by hand and carry an identifier note in the reference list explaining what was found and why it was not adopted.

    Two methodological lessons are recorded because both cost time. A Crossref miss is not proof that an identifier is wrong: the 10.13345 prefix is absent from Crossref but resolves at doi.org, and the AlphaFold 3 addendum is absent from Crossref, which offered an unrelated report with a near-identical title, while Europe PMC found it immediately. And a correct DOI is not evidence of a correct citation, which is the more dangerous of the two, because the DOI resolves and the author name beside it is simply wrong.

  2. Complete author lists. Done for every entry that carries an identifier. The 27 entries still reading “[author list not retrieved]” are company and trade-press items, FDA and Federal Register documents, theses and software servers, for which no registry holds an author list; they print the absence rather than a guess. Replacing these with corporate or agency authorship is a stylistic choice for whoever formats the document, not a verification task.

  3. Re-verify sequences directly against UniProt Done. All 36 accessions in the corpus were re-fetched from the UniProtKB REST API and verified by CRC64 checksum, which establishes sequence identity rather than mere consistency of length and mass. 36 of 36 match and none is a secondary accession. See data/external/sequence_verification*.

  4. Merge the expanded titre corpus and re-run Chapters 5 and 6. Done. The 306-record corpus is merged, Chapter 5 is rebuilt on 75 records over 26 proteins and Chapter 6 on 53 records over 25 proteins, both with Benjamini–Hochberg control, bootstrap intervals and permutation p-values. The disulfide association did not survive it (§6.2.1).

  5. Scan the phosphate and heat-removal bounds, which were carried as an unchecked limitation. Done, in §5.2.4. Phosphate binds only on the caseins and only below about 2 g P L⁻¹ against the 7.3 g L⁻¹ a standard basal salts medium supplies, and it is the only bound that varies strongly between proteins. The heat of product synthesis leaves carbon tighter in every case, but by only 1.49-fold at the low-cooling end, and because the calculation excludes growth and maintenance respiration it overstates its own ceiling. Heat removal at production scale therefore remains a stated open question rather than a closed check.

  6. Re-run disorder with a modern predictor and rebuild the codon reference from highly expressed genes. Done. Disorder is measured with metapredict v3, with FoldIndex retained and reported alongside; the codon reference is the 165-gene highly expressed set from the RefSeq GS115 coding sequences (§3.7).

  7. Format: convert to the institution’s required template, add the declaration and signature pages, and paginate. This is the only remaining task that cannot be done from the repository, because it needs information this analysis does not have; §D.3 lists exactly what.

Appendix F — How a corrected, FDR-controlled correlation turned out to be an artefact

This appendix documents a finding this thesis nearly made. It is kept because the failure is more instructive than the result would have been, and because the audit trail is the thesis’s main claim to being trustworthy about its remaining numbers.

F.1 The finding as reported

An independent analysis of the same literature, with its own curated panel of fourteen dairy, egg and haem proteins and its own computed ceilings, tested 32 sequence features against log₁₀ ceiling utilisation and reported one survivor:

Feature mean metapredict disorder score
Spearman ρ −0.833
Permutation p (20,000 relabellings) 0.00025
Benjamini–Hochberg q across 32 features 0.008
Bootstrap 95% CI −0.98 to −0.45
Leave-one-out ρ across all 14 fits −0.791 to −0.929
Leave-one-out permutation p never above 0.0026

Nothing about that table is wrong as arithmetic. It carries a permutation p-value rather than an asymptotic one, multiple-testing control across every feature tested, a bootstrap interval, and the leave-one-out check that small-n rank correlations are supposed to need. It is better-controlled than most published correlations of its kind. It was also an artefact, and none of those controls could have revealed that, because every one of them tests the statistics while the fault was in the records.

F.2 What the audit found

Two audits ran in parallel on different questions.

The structural audit asked whether the correlation could be a two-cluster artefact. The panel holds two proteins with mean disorder near 0.87 — bovine osteopontin and κ-casein — and twelve between 0.06 and 0.16. A rank correlation across that configuration can be produced entirely by the contrast between the two groups, with the ranks inside the globular group contributing noise. A leave-one-out check is structurally incapable of detecting this, because removing either disordered protein leaves the other in place to hold the contrast up. The discriminating test is whether the association survives within the globular group, and it did not: ρ = −0.455, p = 0.138 on the external panel, ρ = −0.429, p = 0.289 on this thesis’s roster.

The provenance audit went back to the primary sources behind the fourteen titres and found three faults:

  1. A titre that is not a secretion titre. Bovine lactoferrin carried 3,500 mg L⁻¹, the panel’s joint-highest value. The source expressed the protein without a signal sequence, harvested the cell pellet, resuspended it in lysis buffer and recovered inclusion bodies with 6 M urea. It is an intracellular yield and was excluded.
  2. Orthologue pooling in the best-titre join. The join that selected each protein’s best record matched on canonical protein label alone, so human and bovine entries of the same protein pooled. Because every α-lactalbumin and osteopontin record in the corpus is human, the bovine entries silently borrowed human titres. Requiring the source organism to agree dropped five entries — including osteopontin, one of the two proteins the correlation rested on, which had no titre of its own at all.
  3. Species and carrier confusions elsewhere in the same join. A 5,450 mg L⁻¹ “ovalbumin” record is Coturnix coturnix, not Gallus gallus; hen ovalbumin’s best species-matched secreted titre in K. phaffii is 35 mg L⁻¹, which moves it from near the top of the ranking to near the bottom. And the corpus’s only cellobiohydrolase I row is Candida antarctica lipase B expressed on a cellobiohydrolase I carrier, so a name match made the carrier the product and credited it with the whole 10 g L⁻¹.

F.3 The corrected result

With those corrections the association is ρ = −0.483, p = 0.117, with nothing surviving FDR correction, and the analysis that reported it has retracted it. The structural diagnosis is confirmed and sharpened: once osteopontin’s borrowed titre is removed, exactly one protein of twelve sits above 0.4 mean disorder, which is precisely the configuration a leave-one-out cannot touch.

This thesis’s own pipeline was checked for the same three faults. It joins on UniProt accession rather than on protein label, so orthologue pooling cannot occur in it, and an independent check found no record in the merged corpus whose accession disagrees with its stated source organism. It had, however, let the carrier construct through: src/corpus.py excluded fusions by the word “fusion” and this record says “carrier”. That record sat fourth in Table 5.1 at 10 g L⁻¹ and 4.45% of its ceiling. The filter now excludes carriers, chimeras and C-tagged constructs, and the corrected record for the same lipase is its own non-carrier titre of 5.41 g L⁻¹.

F.4 What this is evidence of

Four controls that are normally treated as sufficient — a permutation p-value, FDR correction across the whole feature set, a bootstrap interval and leave-one-out validation — all passed on data containing a non-secretion titre, a borrowed titre and a carrier mass. Statistical controls validate inference from the records; they say nothing about whether the records mean what their column headings say. The two things that did find the fault were a structural test chosen because it could discriminate between two specific explanations, and reading the primary sources behind the individual numbers.

That is also the argument for the corpus design described in §3.9. Every record in titers_merged.tsv carries a verbatim quotation from its source, and it was the quotation on the lactoferrin record — the words “cell lysis, and purification” — that made the first fault findable at all. A corpus of numbers without their sentences would have hidden it.

Appendix G — The prior-art audit in full

§2.8 states the concession. This appendix records the audit that produced it, because a novelty claim rests on the thoroughness of the search that failed to find a competitor, and that search should be inspectable.

G.1 What was searched

The audit screened roughly 220 records with verified identifiers, assembled from four kinds of query run against Europe PMC, Crossref and general web search:

  1. Method queries — combinations of {genome-scale, constraint-based, flux balance, proteome-constrained} with {protein cost, secretion cost, per-protein yield, maximum theoretical yield} and with {Pichia pastoris, Komagataella phaffii, Trichoderma reesei, yeast, CHO}.
  2. Object queries — combinations of {producibility, expressibility, secretability, developability, expression prediction} with {index, score, predictor, sequence-based}.
  3. Panel queries — each of the nine panel proteins by name and by UniProt accession, against {titre, titer, g/L, mg/L, secretion, recombinant production} and against each host.
  4. Concurrent-work queries — public code search for implementations of cost reactions on the iMT1026 lineage, which is how the unpublished repository noted in §2.8 was found.

G.2 What was found, by claim

Component of this thesis Prior art Status
Per-protein biosynthetic cost in a genome-scale model Feizi et al. 2013; Gutierrez et al. 2020 Established. Used as an instrument, cited at the point of use.
Protein-specific secretion reactions with bottleneck attribution pcSecYeast, Li et al. 2022 Established, and more capable than the model used here. Cited as the method’s origin.
Glycosylation cost in a model of this host Irani et al. 2016 Established. Chapter 4’s glycan accounting is an application of it.
Haem supply as a modelled constraint in this host Pentjuss et al. 2023 Established for growth-coupled haem; not applied to leghemoglobin yield.
Sequence-based prediction of expression or secretion Presep 2013; Dykstra et al. 2017; Bhandari et al. 2021; Martiny et al. 2021; Masson et al. 2025; and others Developed field. No index is claimed here.
Composite sequence-based developability scores Lauer et al. 2012 and the biologics tradition Established as a legitimate construct.
Qualitative tractability ranking of milk proteins Guo et al. 2026 Already in print as expert judgement. Used as a pre-registered expectation, §2.9.
Cost reactions on iMT1026v3 in K. phaffii Unpublished public repository, last pushed October 2026 Concurrent independent work on overlapping ground.
Ceiling utilisation: each published titre as a fraction of its own protein’s stoichiometric ceiling None retrieved Claimed.
Within-protein decomposition of the dispersion in realised production None retrieved Claimed.
Quotation-backed titre corpus for these hosts None retrieved Claimed.

G.3 What the audit changed

Two things, and both were costly to the project’s original framing.

It retired the producibility index. The project began intending to build a sequence-derived producibility score for food proteins. The audit established that such an object is not novel, and §6.4 and §5.2.2 subsequently established that it could not have worked on this data in any case, because about half the dispersion it would have to explain occurs at fixed sequence. The second finding is the more interesting one, and it would not have been looked for if the audit had not first removed the reason to build the index.

It narrowed the claim to the measurement and the corpus. What remains is defensible precisely because the audit removed what was not.

G.4 A caveat on negative searches

A search that finds nothing is weaker evidence than a search that finds something, and three specific weaknesses are recorded. Company work is not published, so a developer may have made this measurement internally. Non-English literature was not searched. And a measurement of this kind could exist inside a paper whose title and abstract are about something else, which no query over titles and abstracts would retrieve. The claim is therefore that no retrievable published work makes this measurement, which is the strongest claim the method supports.

References

Verification status. Every identifier in this list was resolved against Crossref and confirmed independently at doi.org. 189 of 230 entries carry a verified DOI; the remaining 41 have none, and the reason is given below rather than left to inference. No identifier in this list was inferred: an earlier audit found that inferred identifiers were wrong roughly half the time, which is why the resolution pass was treated as blocking.

Resolution corrected the record in ways worth stating, because each would have produced a wrong in-text citation. Rebuilding every entry from registry metadata changed 49 author lists, 11 first authors (mostly diacritic losses, but one entry recorded Wang for a paper whose first author is Alderson), 12 years, 3 truncated titles and 1 venue. A second pass over the entries that initially resolved to nothing recovered 48 more identifiers by title search, each re-fetched in full and accepted only on title similarity above 0.97, year within one, agreement of first author where one was recorded, a citable registry type, and live confirmation at doi.org; that pass corrected two further records, one first author and one year. Resolution also exposed two papers that this bibliography had listed twice, now merged. Every change is listed in data/literature/bibliography_corrections.md and doi_candidate_audit.md, with the originally recorded value preserved beside it.

Of the 41 entries without an identifier, the great majority legitimately have none: company and trade-press items, FDA and Federal Register documents, theses, software servers and an edited volume. 27 of them also carry no retrieved author list and say so rather than carrying a guess. Three entries whose automated verdict was “no record” were then searched by hand, and each carries an identifier note explaining what was found and why it was not adopted. One registry failing to find a work is not evidence that the work has no identifier: the AlphaFold 3 addendum is absent from Crossref, which offered an unrelated report with a near-identical title, and was found at once in Europe PMC.

Total entries: 230. With a verified DOI: 189. Peer-reviewed or review: 173.
